abstract: Neurons rely on local mRNA transport to support the metabolic and structural demands of their distal compartments. Synaptojanin 2a (Synj2a), a mitochondria-associated phosphoinositide phosphatase, binds numerous mitochondrial mRNAs via an RNA recognition motif (RRM) and delivers them to axons and dendrites. Among these, PINK1 mRNA transport is particularly critical for mitochondrial quality control. Here we show that this RNA transport function, independent of Synj2s catalytic activity, is required for PINK1-dependent mitochondrial quality control, synaptic bioenergetics, and neuronal resilience. We made mice and human iPSC-derived neurons carrying RRM point mutations that disrupt RNA binding while preserving both phosphatase domains. The mutations also reduced endogenous Synj2 protein levels, indicating that RNA binding contributes to Synj2 stability. Rescue experiments with the RRM targeted to the outer mitochondrial membrane were therefore necessary to isolate which effects are due to RNA-binding. Neurons with the mutated RRM failed to localize PINK1 mRNA to neurites. Consequently, depolarizing mitochondria in these neurites failed to stabilize PINK1 protein or cause phosphoubiquitin to accumulate on mitochondria. Re-expressing the RRM rescued these defects, confirming that RNA-binding rather than phosphatase activity drives the phenotype. Mutant mice showed abnormal mitochondrial cristae ultrastructure and reduced respiratory capacity in synaptosomes. Metabolic profiling revealed extensive reprogramming, most notably increased glycolytic flux, elevated branched-chain amino acids and reduced cholesterol. Despite compensatory reprogramming, mutant neurons showed heightened vulnerability to mitochondrial and excitotoxic stress. This vulnerability was partially rescued by the mitochondrially-targeted RRM. These findings establish Synj2-mediated mRNA transport as a significant mechanism that supports mitochondrial homeostasis.
